1|# QuickStart
2|
3|First, start by importing HTTPX:
4|
5|```pycon
6|>>> import httpx
7|```
8|
9|Now, let’s try to get a webpage.
10|
11|```pycon
12|>>> r = httpx.get('https://httpbin.org/get')
13|>>> r
14|<Response [200 OK]>
15|```
16|
17|Similarly, to make an HTTP POST request:
18|
19|```pycon
20|>>> r = httpx.post('https://httpbin.org/post', data={'key': 'value'})
21|```
22|
23|The PUT, DELETE, HEAD, and OPTIONS requests all follow the same style:
24|
25|```pycon
26|>>> r = httpx.put('https://httpbin.org/put', data={'key': 'value'})
27|>>> r = httpx.delete('https://httpbin.org/delete')
28|>>> r = httpx.head('https://httpbin.org/get')
29|>>> r = httpx.options('https://httpbin.org/get')
30|```
31|
32|## Passing Parameters in URLs
33|
34|To include URL query parameters in the request, use the `params` keyword:
35|
36|```pycon
37|>>> params = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': 'value2'}
38|>>> r = httpx.get('https://httpbin.org/get', params=params)
39|```
40|
41|To see how the values get encoding into the URL string, we can inspect the
42|resulting URL that was used to make the request:
43|
44|```pycon
45|>>> r.url
46|URL('https://httpbin.org/get?key2=value2&key1=value1')
47|```
48|
49|You can also pass a list of items as a value:
50|
51|```pycon
52|>>> params = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': ['value2', 'value3']}
53|>>> r = httpx.get('https://httpbin.org/get', params=params)
54|>>> r.url
55|URL('https://httpbin.org/get?key1=value1&key2=value2&key2=value3')
56|```
57|
58|## Response Content
59|
60|HTTPX will automatically handle decoding the response content into Unicode text.
61|
62|```pycon
63|>>> r = httpx.get('https://www.example.org/')
64|>>> r.text
65|'<!doctype html>\n<html>\n<head>\n<title>Example Domain</title>...'
66|```
67|
68|You can inspect what encoding will be used to decode the response.
69|
70|```pycon
71|>>> r.encoding
72|'UTF-8'
73|```
74|
75|In some cases the response may not contain an explicit encoding, in which case HTTPX
76|will attempt to automatically determine an encoding to use.
77|
78|```pycon
79|>>> r.encoding
80|None
81|>>> r.text
82|'<!doctype html>\n<html>\n<head>\n<title>Example Domain</title>...'
83|```
84|
85|If you need to override the standard behaviour and explicitly set the encoding to
86|use, then you can do that too.
87|
88|```pycon
89|>>> r.encoding = 'ISO-8859-1'
90|```
91|
92|## Binary Response Content
93|
94|The response content can also be accessed as bytes, for non-text responses:
95|
96|```pycon
97|>>> r.content
98|b'<!doctype html>\n<html>\n<head>\n<title>Example Domain</title>...'
99|```
100|
101|Any `gzip` and `deflate` HTTP response encodings will automatically
102|be decoded for you. If `brotlipy` is installed, then the `brotli` response
103|encoding will be supported. If `zstandard` is installed, then `zstd`
104|response encodings will also be supported.
105|
106|For example, to create an image from binary data returned by a request, you can use the following code:
107|
108|```pycon
109|>>> from PIL import Image
110|>>> from io import BytesIO
111|>>> i = Image.open(BytesIO(r.content))
112|```
113|
114|## JSON Response Content
115|
116|Often Web API responses will be encoded as JSON.
117|
118|```pycon
119|>>> r = httpx.get('https://api.github.com/events')
120|>>> r.json()
121|[{u'repository': {u'open_issues': 0, u'url': 'https://github.com/...' ...  }}]
122|```
123|
124|## Custom Headers
125|
126|To include additional headers in the outgoing request, use the `headers` keyword argument:
127|
128|```pycon
129|>>> url = 'https://httpbin.org/headers'
130|>>> headers = {'user-agent': 'my-app/0.0.1'}
131|>>> r = httpx.get(url, headers=headers)
132|```
133|
134|## Sending Form Encoded Data
135|
136|Some types of HTTP requests, such as `POST` and `PUT` requests, can include data
137|in the request body. One common way of including that is as form-encoded data,
138|which is used for HTML forms.
139|
140|```pycon
141|>>> data = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': 'value2'}
142|>>> r = httpx.post("https://httpbin.org/post", data=data)
143|>>> print(r.text)
144|{
145|  ...
146|  "form": {
147|    "key2": "value2",
148|    "key1": "value1"
149|  },
150|  ...
151|}
152|```
153|
154|Form encoded data can also include multiple values from a given key.
155|
156|```pycon
157|>>> data = {'key1': ['value1', 'value2']}
158|>>> r = httpx.post("https://httpbin.org/post", data=data)
159|>>> print(r.text)
160|{
161|  ...
162|  "form": {
163|    "key1": [
164|      "value1",
165|      "value2"
166|    ]
167|  },
168|  ...
169|}
170|```
171|
172|## Sending Multipart File Uploads
173|
174|You can also upload files, using HTTP multipart encoding:
175|
176|```pycon
177|>>> with open('report.xls', 'rb') as report_file:
178|...     files = {'upload-file': report_file}
179|...     r = httpx.post("https://httpbin.org/post", files=files)
180|>>> print(r.text)
181|{
182|  ...
183|  "files": {
184|    "upload-file": "<... binary content ...>"
185|  },
186|  ...
187|}
188|```
189|
190|You can also explicitly set the filename and content type, by using a tuple
191|of items for the file value:
192|
193|```pycon
194|>>> with open('report.xls', 'rb') as report_file:
195|...     files = {'upload-file': ('report.xls', report_file, 'application/vnd.ms-excel')}
196|...     r = httpx.post("https://httpbin.org/post", files=files)
197|>>> print(r.text)
198|{
199|  ...
200|  "files": {
201|    "upload-file": "<... binary content ...>"
202|  },
203|  ...
204|}
205|```
206|
207|If you need to include non-file data fields in the multipart form, use the `data=...` parameter:
208|
209|```pycon
210|>>> data = {'message': 'Hello, world!'}
211|>>> with open('report.xls', 'rb') as report_file:
212|...     files = {'file': report_file}
213|...     r = httpx.post("https://httpbin.org/post", data=data, files=files)
214|>>> print(r.text)
215|{
216|  ...
217|  "files": {
218|    "file": "<... binary content ...>"
219|  },
220|  "form": {
221|    "message": "Hello, world!",
222|  },
223|  ...
224|}
225|```
226|
227|## Sending JSON Encoded Data
228|
229|Form encoded data is okay if all you need is a simple key-value data structure.
230|For more complicated data structures you'll often want to use JSON encoding instead.
231|
232|```pycon
233|>>> data = {'integer': 123, 'boolean': True, 'list': ['a', 'b', 'c']}
234|>>> r = httpx.post("https://httpbin.org/post", json=data)
235|>>> print(r.text)
236|{
237|  ...
238|  "json": {
239|    "boolean": true,
240|    "integer": 123,
241|    "list": [
242|      "a",
243|      "b",
244|      "c"
245|    ]
246|  },
247|  ...
248|}
249|```
250|
251|## Sending Binary Request Data
252|
253|For other encodings, you should use the `content=...` parameter, passing
254|either a `bytes` type or a generator that yields `bytes`.
255|
256|```pycon
257|>>> content = b'Hello, world'
258|>>> r = httpx.post("https://httpbin.org/post", content=content)
259|```
260|
261|You may also want to set a custom `Content-Type` header when uploading
262|binary data.
263|
264|## Response Status Codes
265|
266|We can inspect the HTTP status code of the response:
267|
268|```pycon
269|>>> r = httpx.get('https://httpbin.org/get')
270|>>> r.status_code
271|200
272|```
273|
274|HTTPX also includes an easy shortcut for accessing status codes by their text phrase.
275|
276|```pycon
277|>>> r.status_code == httpx.codes.OK
278|True
279|```
280|
281|We can raise an exception for any responses which are not a 2xx success code:
282|
283|```pycon
284|>>> not_found = httpx.get('https://httpbin.org/status/404')
285|>>> not_found.status_code
286|404
287|>>> not_found.raise_for_status()
288|Traceback (most recent call last):
289|  File "/Users/tomchristie/GitHub/encode/httpcore/httpx/models.py", line 837, in raise_for_status
290|    raise HTTPStatusError(message, response=self)
291|httpx._exceptions.HTTPStatusError: 404 Client Error: Not Found for url: https://httpbin.org/status/404
292|For more information check: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/404
293|```
294|
295|Any successful response codes will return the `Response` instance rather than raising an exception.
296|
297|```pycon
298|>>> r.raise_for_status()
299|```
300|
301|The method returns the response instance, allowing you to use it inline. For example:
302|
303|```pycon
304|>>> r = httpx.get('...').raise_for_status()
305|>>> data = httpx.get('...').raise_for_status().json()
306|```
307|
308|## Response Headers
309|
310|The response headers are available as a dictionary-like interface.
311|
312|```pycon
313|>>> r.headers
314|Headers({
315|    'content-encoding': 'gzip',
316|    'transfer-encoding': 'chunked',
317|    'connection': 'close',
318|    'server': 'nginx/1.0.4',
319|    'x-runtime': '148ms',
320|    'etag': '"e1ca502697e5c9317743dc078f67693f"',
321|    'content-type': 'application/json'
322|})
323|```
324|
325|The `Headers` data type is case-insensitive, so you can use any capitalization.
326|
327|```pycon
328|>>> r.headers['Content-Type']
329|'application/json'
330|
331|>>> r.headers.get('content-type')
332|'application/json'
333|```
334|
335|Multiple values for a single response header are represented as a single comma-separated value, as per [RFC 7230](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2):
336|
337|> A recipient MAY combine multiple header fields with the same field name into one “field-name: field-value” pair, without changing the semantics of the message, by appending each subsequent field-value to the combined field value in order, separated by a comma.
338|
339|## Streaming Responses
340|
341|For large downloads you may want to use streaming responses that do not load the entire response body into memory at once.
342|
343|You can stream the binary content of the response...
344|
345|```pycon
346|>>> with httpx.stream("GET", "https://www.example.com") as r:
347|...     for data in r.iter_bytes():
348|...         print(data)
349|```
350|
351|Or the text of the response...
352|
353|```pycon
354|>>> with httpx.stream("GET", "https://www.example.com") as r:
355|...     for text in r.iter_text():
356|...         print(text)
357|```
358|
359|Or stream the text, on a line-by-line basis...
360|
361|```pycon
362|>>> with httpx.stream("GET", "https://www.example.com") as r:
363|...     for line in r.iter_lines():
364|...         print(line)
365|```
366|
367|HTTPX will use universal line endings, normalising all cases to `\n`.
368|
369|In some cases you might want to access the raw bytes on the response without applying any HTTP content decoding. In this case any content encoding that the web server has applied such as `gzip`, `deflate`, `brotli`, or `zstd` will
370|not be automatically decoded.
371|
372|```pycon
373|>>> with httpx.stream("GET", "https://www.example.com") as r:
374|...     for chunk in r.iter_raw():
375|...         print(chunk)
376|```
377|
378|If you're using streaming responses in any of these ways then the `response.content` and `response.text` attributes will not be available, and will raise errors if accessed. However you can also use the response streaming functionality to conditionally load the response body:
379|
380|```pycon
381|>>> with httpx.stream("GET", "https://www.example.com") as r:
382|...     if int(r.headers['Content-Length']) < TOO_LONG:
383|...         r.read()
384|...         print(r.text)
385|```
386|
387|## Cookies
388|
389|Any cookies that are set on the response can be easily accessed:
390|
391|```pycon
392|>>> r = httpx.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies/set?chocolate=chip')
393|>>> r.cookies['chocolate']
394|'chip'
395|```
396|
397|To include cookies in an outgoing request, use the `cookies` parameter:
398|
399|```pycon
400|>>> cookies = {"peanut": "butter"}
401|>>> r = httpx.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies', cookies=cookies)
402|>>> r.json()
403|{'cookies': {'peanut': 'butter'}}
404|```
405|
406|Cookies are returned in a `Cookies` instance, which is a dict-like data structure
407|with additional API for accessing cookies by their domain or path.
408|
409|```pycon
410|>>> cookies = httpx.Cookies()
411|>>> cookies.set('cookie_on_domain', 'hello, there!', domain='httpbin.org')
412|>>> cookies.set('cookie_off_domain', 'nope.', domain='example.org')
413|>>> r = httpx.get('http://httpbin.org/cookies', cookies=cookies)
414|>>> r.json()
415|{'cookies': {'cookie_on_domain': 'hello, there!'}}
416|```
417|
418|## Redirection and History
419|
420|By default, HTTPX will **not** follow redirects for all HTTP methods, although
421|this can be explicitly enabled.
422|
423|For example, GitHub redirects all HTTP requests to HTTPS.
424|
425|```pycon
426|>>> r = httpx.get('http://github.com/')
427|>>> r.status_code
428|301
429|>>> r.history
430|[]
431|>>> r.next_request
432|<Request('GET', 'https://github.com/')>
433|```
434|
435|You can modify the default redirection handling with the `follow_redirects` parameter:
436|
437|```pycon
438|>>> r = httpx.get('http://github.com/', follow_redirects=True)
439|>>> r.url
440|URL('https://github.com/')
441|>>> r.status_code
442|200
443|>>> r.history
444|[<Response [301 Moved Permanently]>]
445|```
446|
447|The `history` property of the response can be used to inspect any followed redirects.
448|It contains a list of any redirect responses that were followed, in the order
449|in which they were made.
450|
451|## Timeouts
452|
453|HTTPX defaults to including reasonable timeouts for all network operations,
454|meaning that if a connection is not properly established then it should always
455|raise an error rather than hanging indefinitely.
456|
457|The default timeout for network inactivity is five seconds. You can modify the
458|value to be more or less strict:
459|
460|```pycon
461|>>> httpx.get('https://github.com/', timeout=0.001)
462|```
463|
464|You can also disable the timeout behavior completely...
465|
466|```pycon
467|>>> httpx.get('https://github.com/', timeout=None)
468|```
469|
470|For advanced timeout management, see [Timeout fine-tuning](advanced/timeouts.md#fine-tuning-the-configuration).
471|
472|## Authentication
473|
474|HTTPX supports Basic and Digest HTTP authentication.
475|
476|To provide Basic authentication credentials, pass a 2-tuple of
477|plaintext `str` or `bytes` objects as the `auth` argument to the request
478|functions:
479|
480|```pycon
481|>>> httpx.get("https://example.com", auth=("my_user", "password123"))
482|```
483|
484|To provide credentials for Digest authentication you'll need to instantiate
485|a `DigestAuth` object with the plaintext username and password as arguments.
486|This object can be then passed as the `auth` argument to the request methods
487|as above:
488|
489|```pycon
490|>>> auth = httpx.DigestAuth("my_user", "password123")
491|>>> httpx.get("https://example.com", auth=auth)
492|<Response [200 OK]>
493|```
494|
495|## Exceptions
496|
497|HTTPX will raise exceptions if an error occurs.
498|
499|The most important exception classes in HTTPX are `RequestError` and `HTTPStatusError`.
500|
501|The `RequestError` class is a superclass that encompasses any exception that occurs
502|while issuing an HTTP request. These exceptions include a `.request` attribute.
503|
504|```python
505|try:
506|    response = httpx.get("https://www.example.com/")
507|except httpx.RequestError as exc:
508|    print(f"An error occurred while requesting {exc.request.url!r}.")
509|```
510|
511|The `HTTPStatusError` class is raised by `response.raise_for_status()` on responses which are not a 2xx success code.
512|These exceptions include both a `.request` and a `.response` attribute.
513|
514|```python
515|response = httpx.get("https://www.example.com/")
516|try:
517|    response.raise_for_status()
518|except httpx.HTTPStatusError as exc:
519|    print(f"Error response {exc.response.status_code} while requesting {exc.request.url!r}.")
520|```
521|
522|There is also a base class `HTTPError` that includes both of these categories, and can be used
523|to catch either failed requests, or 4xx and 5xx responses.
524|
525|You can either use this base class to catch both categories...
526|
527|```python
528|try:
529|    response = httpx.get("https://www.example.com/")
530|    response.raise_for_status()
531|except httpx.HTTPError as exc:
532|    print(f"Error while requesting {exc.request.url!r}.")
533|```
534|
535|Or handle each case explicitly...
536|
537|```python
538|try:
539|    response = httpx.get("https://www.example.com/")
540|    response.raise_for_status()
541|except httpx.RequestError as exc:
542|    print(f"An error occurred while requesting {exc.request.url!r}.")
543|except httpx.HTTPStatusError as exc:
544|    print(f"Error response {exc.response.status_code} while requesting {exc.request.url!r}.")
545|```
546|
547|For a full list of available exceptions, see [Exceptions (API Reference)](exceptions.md).

1|HTTPX's `Client` also accepts a `transport` argument. This argument allows you
2|to provide a custom Transport object that will be used to perform the actual
3|sending of the requests.
4|
5|## HTTP Transport
6|
7|For some advanced configuration you might need to instantiate a transport
8|class directly, and pass it to the client instance. One example is the
9|`local_address` configuration which is only available via this low-level API.
10|
11|```pycon
12|>>> import httpx
13|>>> transport = httpx.HTTPTransport(local_address="0.0.0.0")
14|>>> client = httpx.Client(transport=transport)
15|```
16|
17|Connection retries are also available via this interface. Requests will be retried the given number of times in case an `httpx.ConnectError` or an `httpx.ConnectTimeout` occurs, allowing smoother operation under flaky networks. If you need other forms of retry behaviors, such as handling read/write errors or reacting to `503 Service Unavailable`, consider general-purpose tools such as [tenacity](https://github.com/jd/tenacity).
18|
19|```pycon
20|>>> import httpx
21|>>> transport = httpx.HTTPTransport(retries=1)
22|>>> client = httpx.Client(transport=transport)
23|```
24|
25|Similarly, instantiating a transport directly provides a `uds` option for
26|connecting via a Unix Domain Socket that is only available via this low-level API:
27|
28|```pycon
29|>>> import httpx
30|>>> # Connect to the Docker API via a Unix Socket.
31|>>> transport = httpx.HTTPTransport(uds="/var/run/docker.sock")
32|>>> client = httpx.Client(transport=transport)
33|>>> response = client.get("http://docker/info")
34|>>> response.json()
35|{"ID": "...", "Containers": 4, "Images": 74, ...}
36|```
37|
38|## WSGI Transport
39|
40|You can configure an `httpx` client to call directly into a Python web application using the WSGI protocol.
41|
42|This is particularly useful for two main use-cases:
43|
44|* Using `httpx` as a client inside test cases.
45|* Mocking out external services during tests or in dev or staging environments.
46|
47|### Example
48|
49|Here's an example of integrating against a Flask application:
50|
51|```python
52|from flask import Flask
53|import httpx
54|
55|
56|app = Flask(__name__)
57|
58|@app.route("/")
59|def hello():
60|    return "Hello World!"
61|
62|transport = httpx.WSGITransport(app=app)
63|with httpx.Client(transport=transport, base_url="http://testserver") as client:
64|    r = client.get("/")
65|    assert r.status_code == 200
66|    assert r.text == "Hello World!"
67|```
68|
69|### Configuration
70|
71|For some more complex cases you might need to customize the WSGI transport. This allows you to:
72|
73|* Inspect 500 error responses rather than raise exceptions by setting `raise_app_exceptions=False`.
74|* Mount the WSGI application at a subpath by setting `script_name` (WSGI).
75|* Use a given client address for requests by setting `remote_addr` (WSGI).
76|
77|For example:
78|
79|```python
80|# Instantiate a client that makes WSGI requests with a client IP of "1.2.3.4".
81|transport = httpx.WSGITransport(app=app, remote_addr="1.2.3.4")
82|with httpx.Client(transport=transport, base_url="http://testserver") as client:
83|    ...
84|```
85|
86|## ASGI Transport
87|
88|You can configure an `httpx` client to call directly into an async Python web application using the ASGI protocol.
89|
90|This is particularly useful for two main use-cases:
91|
92|* Using `httpx` as a client inside test cases.
93|* Mocking out external services during tests or in dev or staging environments.
94|
95|### Example
96|
97|Let's take this Starlette application as an example:
98|
99|```python
100|from starlette.applications import Starlette
101|from starlette.responses import HTMLResponse
102|from starlette.routing import Route
103|
104|
105|async def hello(request):
106|    return HTMLResponse("Hello World!")
107|
108|
109|app = Starlette(routes=[Route("/", hello)])
110|```
111|
112|We can make requests directly against the application, like so:
113|
114|```python
115|transport = httpx.ASGITransport(app=app)
116|
117|async with httpx.AsyncClient(transport=transport, base_url="http://testserver") as client:
118|    r = await client.get("/")
119|    assert r.status_code == 200
120|    assert r.text == "Hello World!"
121|```
122|
123|### Configuration
124|
125|For some more complex cases you might need to customise the ASGI transport. This allows you to:
126|
127|* Inspect 500 error responses rather than raise exceptions by setting `raise_app_exceptions=False`.
128|* Mount the ASGI application at a subpath by setting `root_path`.
129|* Use a given client address for requests by setting `client`.
130|
131|For example:
132|
133|```python
134|# Instantiate a client that makes ASGI requests with a client IP of "1.2.3.4",
135|# on port 123.
136|transport = httpx.ASGITransport(app=app, client=("1.2.3.4", 123))
137|async with httpx.AsyncClient(transport=transport, base_url="http://testserver") as client:
138|    ...
139|```
140|
141|See [the ASGI documentation](https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/specs/www.html#connection-scope) for more details on the `client` and `root_path` keys.
142|
143|### ASGI startup and shutdown
144|
145|It is not in the scope of HTTPX to trigger ASGI lifespan events of your app.
146|
147|However it is suggested to use `LifespanManager` from [asgi-lifespan](https://github.com/florimondmanca/asgi-lifespan#usage) in pair with `AsyncClient`.
148|
149|## Custom transports
150|
151|A transport instance must implement the low-level Transport API which deals
152|with sending a single request, and returning a response. You should either
153|subclass `httpx.BaseTransport` to implement a transport to use with `Client`,
154|or subclass `httpx.AsyncBaseTransport` to implement a transport to
155|use with `AsyncClient`.
156|
157|At the layer of the transport API we're using the familiar `Request` and
158|`Response` models.
159|
160|See the `handle_request` and `handle_async_request` docstrings for more details
161|on the specifics of the Transport API.
162|
163|A complete example of a custom transport implementation would be:
164|
165|```python
166|import json
167|import httpx
168|
169|class HelloWorldTransport(httpx.BaseTransport):
170|    """
171|    A mock transport that always returns a JSON "Hello, world!" response.
172|    """
173|
174|    def handle_request(self, request):
175|        return httpx.Response(200, json={"text": "Hello, world!"})
176|```
177|
178|Or this example, which uses a custom transport and `httpx.Mounts` to always redirect `http://` requests.
179|
180|```python
181|class HTTPSRedirect(httpx.BaseTransport):
182|    """
183|    A transport that always redirects to HTTPS.
184|    """
185|    def handle_request(self, request):
186|        url = request.url.copy_with(scheme="https")
187|        return httpx.Response(303, headers={"Location": str(url)})
188|
189|# A client where any `http` requests are always redirected to `https`
190|transport = httpx.Mounts({
191|    'http://': HTTPSRedirect()
192|    'https://': httpx.HTTPTransport()
193|})
194|client = httpx.Client(transport=transport)
195|```
196|
197|A useful pattern here is custom transport classes that wrap the default HTTP implementation. For example...
198|
199|```python
200|class DebuggingTransport(httpx.BaseTransport):
201|    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
202|        self._wrapper = httpx.HTTPTransport(**kwargs)
203|
204|    def handle_request(self, request):
205|        print(f">>> {request}")
206|        response = self._wrapper.handle_request(request)
207|        print(f"<<< {response}")
208|        return response
209|
210|    def close(self):
211|        self._wrapper.close()
212|
213|transport = DebuggingTransport()
214|client = httpx.Client(transport=transport)
215|```
216|
217|Here's another case, where we're using a round-robin across a number of different proxies...
218|
219|```python
220|class ProxyRoundRobin(httpx.BaseTransport):
221|    def __init__(self, proxies, **kwargs):
222|        self._transports = [
223|            httpx.HTTPTransport(proxy=proxy, **kwargs)
224|            for proxy in proxies
225|        ]
226|        self._idx = 0
227|
228|    def handle_request(self, request):
229|        transport = self._transports[self._idx]
230|        self._idx = (self._idx + 1) % len(self._transports)
231|        return transport.handle_request(request)
232|
233|    def close(self):
234|        for transport in self._transports:
235|            transport.close()
236|
237|proxies = [
238|    httpx.Proxy("http://127.0.0.1:8081"),
239|    httpx.Proxy("http://127.0.0.1:8082"),
240|    httpx.Proxy("http://127.0.0.1:8083"),
241|]
242|transport = ProxyRoundRobin(proxies=proxies)
243|client = httpx.Client(transport=transport)
244|```
245|
246|## Mock transports
247|
248|During testing it can often be useful to be able to mock out a transport,
249|and return pre-determined responses, rather than making actual network requests.
250|
251|The `httpx.MockTransport` class accepts a handler function, which can be used
252|to map requests onto pre-determined responses:
253|
254|```python
255|def handler(request):
256|    return httpx.Response(200, json={"text": "Hello, world!"})
257|
258|
259|# Switch to a mock transport, if the TESTING environment variable is set.
260|if os.environ.get('TESTING', '').upper() == "TRUE":
261|    transport = httpx.MockTransport(handler)
262|else:
263|    transport = httpx.HTTPTransport()
264|
265|client = httpx.Client(transport=transport)
266|```
267|
268|For more advanced use-cases you might want to take a look at either [the third-party
269|mocking library, RESPX](https://lundberg.github.io/respx/), or the [pytest-httpx library](https://github.com/Colin-b/pytest_httpx).
270|
271|## Mounting transports
272|
273|You can also mount transports against given schemes or domains, to control
274|which transport an outgoing request should be routed via, with [the same style
275|used for specifying proxy routing](#routing).
276|
277|```python
278|import httpx
279|
280|class HTTPSRedirectTransport(httpx.BaseTransport):
281|    """
282|    A transport that always redirects to HTTPS.
283|    """
284|
285|    def handle_request(self, method, url, headers, stream, extensions):
286|        scheme, host, port, path = url
287|        if port is None:
288|            location = b"https://%s%s" % (host, path)
289|        else:
290|            location = b"https://%s:%d%s" % (host, port, path)
291|        stream = httpx.ByteStream(b"")
292|        headers = [(b"location", location)]
293|        extensions = {}
294|        return 303, headers, stream, extensions
295|
296|
297|# A client where any `http` requests are always redirected to `https`
298|mounts = {'http://': HTTPSRedirectTransport()}
299|client = httpx.Client(mounts=mounts)
300|```
301|
302|A couple of other sketches of how you might take advantage of mounted transports...
303|
304|Disabling HTTP/2 on a single given domain...
305|
306|```python
307|mounts = {
308|    "all://": httpx.HTTPTransport(http2=True),
309|    "all://*example.org": httpx.HTTPTransport()
310|}
311|client = httpx.Client(mounts=mounts)
312|```
313|
314|Mocking requests to a given domain:
315|
316|```python
317|# All requests to "example.org" should be mocked out.
318|# Other requests occur as usual.
319|def handler(request):
320|    return httpx.Response(200, json={"text": "Hello, World!"})
321|
322|mounts = {"all://example.org": httpx.MockTransport(handler)}
323|client = httpx.Client(mounts=mounts)
324|```
325|
326|Adding support for custom schemes:
327|
328|```python
329|# Support URLs like "file:///Users/sylvia_green/websites/new_client/index.html"
330|mounts = {"file://": FileSystemTransport()}
331|client = httpx.Client(mounts=mounts)
332|```
333|
334|### Routing
335|
336|HTTPX provides a powerful mechanism for routing requests, allowing you to write complex rules that specify which transport should be used for each request.
337|
338|The `mounts` dictionary maps URL patterns to HTTP transports. HTTPX matches requested URLs against URL patterns to decide which transport should be used, if any. Matching is done from most specific URL patterns (e.g. `https://<domain>:<port>`) to least specific ones (e.g. `https://`).
339|
340|HTTPX supports routing requests based on **scheme**, **domain**, **port**, or a combination of these.
341|
342|### Wildcard routing
343|
344|Route everything through a transport...
345|
346|```python
347|mounts = {
348|    "all://": httpx.HTTPTransport(proxy="http://localhost:8030"),
349|}
350|```
351|
352|### Scheme routing
353|
354|Route HTTP requests through one transport, and HTTPS requests through another...
355|
356|```python
357|mounts = {
358|    "http://": httpx.HTTPTransport(proxy="http://localhost:8030"),
359|    "https://": httpx.HTTPTransport(proxy="http://localhost:8031"),
360|}
361|```
362|
363|### Domain routing
364|
365|Proxy all requests on domain "example.com", let other requests pass through...
366|
367|```python
368|mounts = {
369|    "all://example.com": httpx.HTTPTransport(proxy="http://localhost:8030"),
370|}
371|```
372|
373|Proxy HTTP requests on domain "example.com", let HTTPS and other requests pass through...
374|
375|```python
376|mounts = {
377|    "http://example.com": httpx.HTTPTransport(proxy="http://localhost:8030"),
378|}
379|```
380|
381|Proxy all requests to "example.com" and its subdomains, let other requests pass through...
382|
383|```python
384|mounts = {
385|    "all://*example.com": httpx.HTTPTransport(proxy="http://localhost:8030"),
386|}
387|```
388|
389|Proxy all requests to strict subdomains of "example.com", let "example.com" and other requests pass through...
390|
391|```python
392|mounts = {
393|    "all://*.example.com": httpx.HTTPTransport(proxy="http://localhost:8030"),
394|}
395|```
396|
397|### Port routing
398|
399|Proxy HTTPS requests on port 1234 to "example.com"...
400|
401|```python
402|mounts = {
403|    "https://example.com:1234": httpx.HTTPTransport(proxy="http://localhost:8030"),
404|}
405|```
406|
407|Proxy all requests on port 1234...
408|
409|```python
410|mounts = {
411|    "all://*:1234": httpx.HTTPTransport(proxy="http://localhost:8030"),
412|}
413|```
414|
415|### No-proxy support
416|
417|It is also possible to define requests that _shouldn't_ be routed through the transport.
418|
419|To do so, pass `None` as the proxy URL. For example...
420|
421|```python
422|mounts = {
423|    # Route requests through a proxy by default...
424|    "all://": httpx.HTTPTransport(proxy="http://localhost:8031"),
425|    # Except those for "example.com".
426|    "all://example.com": None,
427|}
428|```
429|
430|### Complex configuration example
431|
432|You can combine the routing features outlined above to build complex proxy routing configurations. For example...
433|
434|```python
435|mounts = {
436|    # Route all traffic through a proxy by default...
437|    "all://": httpx.HTTPTransport(proxy="http://localhost:8030"),
438|    # But don't use proxies for HTTPS requests to "domain.io"...
439|    "https://domain.io": None,
440|    # And use another proxy for requests to "example.com" and its subdomains...
441|    "all://*example.com": httpx.HTTPTransport(proxy="http://localhost:8031"),
442|    # And yet another proxy if HTTP is used,
443|    # and the "internal" subdomain on port 5550 is requested...
444|    "http://internal.example.com:5550": httpx.HTTPTransport(proxy="http://localhost:8032"),
445|}
446|```
447|
448|### Environment variables
449|
450|There are also environment variables that can be used to control the dictionary of the client mounts. 
451|They can be used to configure HTTP proxying for clients.
452|
453|See documentation on [`HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY`](../environment_variables.md#http_proxy-https_proxy-all_proxy)
454|and [`NO_PROXY`](../environment_variables.md#no_proxy) for more information.

63|class ASGITransport(AsyncBaseTransport):
64|    """
65|    A custom AsyncTransport that handles sending requests directly to an ASGI app.
66|
67|    ```python
68|    transport = httpx.ASGITransport(
69|        app=app,
70|        root_path="/submount",
71|        client=("1.2.3.4", 123)
72|    )
73|    client = httpx.AsyncClient(transport=transport)

75|
76|    Arguments:
77|
78|    * `app` - The ASGI application.
79|    * `raise_app_exceptions` - Boolean indicating if exceptions in the application
80|       should be raised. Default to `True`. Can be set to `False` for use cases
81|       such as testing the content of a client 500 response.
82|    * `root_path` - The root path on which the ASGI application should be mounted.
83|    * `client` - A two-tuple indicating the client IP and port of incoming requests.
84|    ```
85|    """

87|    def __init__(
88|        self,
89|        app: _ASGIApp,
90|        raise_app_exceptions: bool = True,
91|        root_path: str = "",
92|        client: tuple[str, int] = ("127.0.0.1", 123),
93|    ) -> None:
94|        self.app = app
95|        self.raise_app_exceptions = raise_app_exceptions
96|        self.root_path = root_path
97|        self.client = client
98|
99|    async def handle_async_request(
100|        self,
101|        request: Request,
102|    ) -> Response:
103|        assert isinstance(request.stream, AsyncByteStream)
104|
105|        # ASGI scope.
106|        scope = {
107|            "type": "http",
108|            "asgi": {"version": "3.0"},
109|            "http_version": "1.1",
110|            "method": request.method,
111|            "headers": [(k.lower(), v) for (k, v) in request.headers.raw],
112|            "scheme": request.url.scheme,
113|            "path": request.url.path,
114|            "raw_path": request.url.raw_path.split(b"?")[0],
115|            "query_string": request.url.query,
116|            "server": (request.url.host, request.url.port),
117|            "client": self.client,
118|            "root_path": self.root_path,
119|        }
120|
121|        # Request.
122|        request_body_chunks = request.stream.__aiter__()
123|        request_complete = False
124|
125|        # Response.
126|        status_code = None
127|        response_headers = None
128|        body_parts = []
129|        response_started = False
130|        response_complete = create_event()
131|
132|        # ASGI callables.
133|
134|        async def receive() -> dict[str, typing.Any]:
135|            nonlocal request_complete
136|
137|            if request_complete:
138|                await response_complete.wait()
139|                return {"type": "http.disconnect"}
140|
141|            try:
142|                body = await request_body_chunks.__anext__()
143|            except StopAsyncIteration:
144|                request_complete = True
145|                return {"type": "http.request", "body": b"", "more_body": False}
146|            return {"type": "http.request", "body": body, "more_body": True}
147|
148|        async def send(message: typing.MutableMapping[str, typing.Any]) -> None:
149|            nonlocal status_code, response_headers, response_started
150|
151|            if message["type"] == "http.response.start":
152|                assert not response_started
153|
154|                status_code = message["status"]
155|                response_headers = message.get("headers", [])
156|                response_started = True
157|
158|            elif message["type"] == "http.response.body":
159|                assert not response_complete.is_set()
160|                body = message.get("body", b"")
161|                more_body = message.get("more_body", False)
162|
163|                if body and request.method != "HEAD":
164|                    body_parts.append(body)
165|
166|                if not more_body:
167|                    response_complete.set()
168|
169|        try:
170|            await self.app(scope, receive, send)
171|        except Exception:  # noqa: PIE-786
172|            if self.raise_app_exceptions:
173|                raise
174|
175|            response_complete.set()
176|            if status_code is None:
177|                status_code = 500
178|            if response_headers is None:
179|                response_headers = {}
180|
181|        assert response_complete.is_set()
182|        assert status_code is not None
183|        assert response_headers is not None
184|
185|        stream = ASGIResponseStream(body_parts)
186|
187|        return Response(status_code, headers=response_headers, stream=stream)

1|!!! hint
2|    If you are coming from Requests, `httpx.Client()` is what you can use instead of `requests.Session()`.
3|
4|## Why use a Client?
5|
6|!!! note "TL;DR"
7|    If you do anything more than experimentation, one-off scripts, or prototypes, then you should use a `Client` instance.
8|
9|**More efficient usage of network resources**
10|
11|When you make requests using the top-level API as documented in the [Quickstart](../quickstart.md) guide, HTTPX has to establish a new connection _for every single request_ (connections are not reused). As the number of requests to a host increases, this quickly becomes inefficient.
12|
13|On the other hand, a `Client` instance uses [HTTP connection pooling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP_persistent_connection). This means that when you make several requests to the same host, the `Client` will reuse the underlying TCP connection, instead of recreating one for every single request.
14|
15|This can bring **significant performance improvements** compared to using the top-level API, including:
16|
17|- Reduced latency across requests (no handshaking).
18|- Reduced CPU usage and round-trips.
19|- Reduced network congestion.
20|
21|**Extra features**
22|
23|`Client` instances also support features that aren't available at the top-level API, such as:
24|
25|- Cookie persistence across requests.
26|- Applying configuration across all outgoing requests.
27|- Sending requests through HTTP proxies.
28|- Using [HTTP/2](../http2.md).
29|
30|The other sections on this page go into further detail about what you can do with a `Client` instance.
31|
32|## Usage
33|
34|The recommended way to use a `Client` is as a context manager. This will ensure that connections are properly cleaned up when leaving the `with` block:
35|
36|```python
37|with httpx.Client() as client:
38|    ...
39|```
40|
41|Alternatively, you can explicitly close the connection pool without block-usage using `.close()`:
42|
43|```python
44|client = httpx.Client()
45|try:
46|    ...
47|finally:
48|    client.close()
49|```
50|
51|## Making requests
52|
53|Once you have a `Client`, you can send requests using `.get()`, `.post()`, etc. For example:
54|
55|```pycon
56|>>> with httpx.Client() as client:
57|...     r = client.get('https://example.com')
58|...
59|>>> r
60|<Response [200 OK]>
61|```
62|
63|These methods accept the same arguments as `httpx.get()`, `httpx.post()`, etc. This means that all features documented in the [Quickstart](../quickstart.md) guide are also available at the client level.
64|
65|For example, to send a request with custom headers:
66|
67|```pycon
68|>>> with httpx.Client() as client:
69|...     headers = {'X-Custom': 'value'}
70|...     r = client.get('https://example.com', headers=headers)
71|...
72|>>> r.request.headers['X-Custom']
73|'value'
74|```
75|
76|## Sharing configuration across requests
77|
78|Clients allow you to apply configuration to all outgoing requests by passing parameters to the `Client` constructor.
79|
80|For example, to apply a set of custom headers _on every request_:
81|
82|```pycon
83|>>> url = 'http://httpbin.org/headers'
84|>>> headers = {'user-agent': 'my-app/0.0.1'}
85|>>> with httpx.Client(headers=headers) as client:
86|...     r = client.get(url)
87|...
88|>>> r.json()['headers']['User-Agent']
89|'my-app/0.0.1'
90|```
91|
92|## Merging of configuration
93|
94|When a configuration option is provided at both the client-level and request-level, one of two things can happen:
95|
96|- For headers, query parameters and cookies, the values are combined together. For example:
97|
98|```pycon
99|>>> headers = {'X-Auth': 'from-client'}
100|>>> params = {'client_id': 'client1'}
101|>>> with httpx.Client(headers=headers, params=params) as client:
102|...     headers = {'X-Custom': 'from-request'}
103|...     params = {'request_id': 'request1'}
104|...     r = client.get('https://example.com', headers=headers, params=params)
105|...
106|>>> r.request.url
107|URL('https://example.com?client_id=client1&request_id=request1')
108|>>> r.request.headers['X-Auth']
109|'from-client'
110|>>> r.request.headers['X-Custom']
111|'from-request'
112|```
113|
114|- For all other parameters, the request-level value takes priority. For example:
115|
116|```pycon
117|>>> with httpx.Client(auth=('tom', 'mot123')) as client:
118|...     r = client.get('https://example.com', auth=('alice', 'ecila123'))
119|...
120|>>> _, _, auth = r.request.headers['Authorization'].partition(' ')
121|>>> import base64
122|>>> base64.b64decode(auth)
123|b'alice:ecila123'
124|```
125|
126|If you need finer-grained control on the merging of client-level and request-level parameters, see [Request instances](#request-instances).
127|
128|## Other Client-only configuration options
129|
130|Additionally, `Client` accepts some configuration options that aren't available at the request level.
131|
132|For example, `base_url` allows you to prepend an URL to all outgoing requests:
133|
134|```pycon
135|>>> with httpx.Client(base_url='http://httpbin.org') as client:
136|...     r = client.get('/headers')
137|...
138|>>> r.request.url
139|URL('http://httpbin.org/headers')
140|```
141|
142|For a list of all available client parameters, see the [`Client`](../api.md#client) API reference.
143|
144|---
145|
146|## Request instances
147|
148|For maximum control on what gets sent over the wire, HTTPX supports building explicit [`Request`](../api.md#request) instances:
149|
150|```python
151|request = httpx.Request("GET", "https://example.com")
152|```
153|
154|To dispatch a `Request` instance across to the network, create a [`Client` instance](#client-instances) and use `.send()`:
155|
156|```python
157|with httpx.Client() as client:
158|    response = client.send(request)
159|    ...
160|```
161|
162|If you need to mix client-level and request-level options in a way that is not supported by the default [Merging of parameters](#merging-of-parameters), you can use `.build_request()` and then make arbitrary modifications to the `Request` instance. For example:
163|
164|```python
165|headers = {"X-Api-Key": "...", "X-Client-ID": "ABC123"}
166|
167|with httpx.Client(headers=headers) as client:
168|    request = client.build_request("GET", "https://api.example.com")
169|
170|    print(request.headers["X-Client-ID"])  # "ABC123"
171|
172|    # Don't send the API key for this particular request.
173|    del request.headers["X-Api-Key"]
174|
175|    response = client.send(request)
176|    ...
177|```
178|
179|## Monitoring download progress
180|
181|If you need to monitor download progress of large responses, you can use response streaming and inspect the `response.num_bytes_downloaded` property.
182|
183|This interface is required for properly determining download progress, because the total number of bytes returned by `response.content` or `response.iter_content()` will not always correspond with the raw content length of the response if HTTP response compression is being used.
184|
185|For example, showing a progress bar using the [`tqdm`](https://github.com/tqdm/tqdm) library while a response is being downloaded could be done like this…
186|
187|```python
188|import tempfile
189|
190|import httpx
191|from tqdm import tqdm
192|
193|with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile() as download_file:
194|    url = "https://speed.hetzner.de/100MB.bin"
195|    with httpx.stream("GET", url) as response:
196|        total = int(response.headers["Content-Length"])
197|
198|        with tqdm(total=total, unit_scale=True, unit_divisor=1024, unit="B") as progress:
199|            num_bytes_downloaded = response.num_bytes_downloaded
200|            for chunk in response.iter_bytes():
201|                download_file.write(chunk)
202|                progress.update(response.num_bytes_downloaded - num_bytes_downloaded)
203|                num_bytes_downloaded = response.num_bytes_downloaded
204|```
205|
206|![tqdm progress bar](../img/tqdm-progress.gif)
207|
208|Or an alternate example, this time using the [`rich`](https://github.com/willmcgugan/rich) library…
209|
210|```python
211|import tempfile
212|import httpx
213|import rich.progress
214|
215|with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile() as download_file:
216|    url = "https://speed.hetzner.de/100MB.bin"
217|    with httpx.stream("GET", url) as response:
218|        total = int(response.headers["Content-Length"])
219|
220|        with rich.progress.Progress(
221|            "[progress.percentage]{task.percentage:>3.0f}%",
222|            rich.progress.BarColumn(bar_width=None),
223|            rich.progress.DownloadColumn(),
224|            rich.progress.TransferSpeedColumn(),
225|        ) as progress:
226|            download_task = progress.add_task("Download", total=total)
227|            for chunk in response.iter_bytes():
228|                download_file.write(chunk)
229|                progress.update(download_task, completed=response.num_bytes_downloaded)
230|```
231|
232|![rich progress bar](../img/rich-progress.gif)
233|
234|## Monitoring upload progress
235|
236|If you need to monitor upload progress of large responses, you can use request content generator streaming.
237|
238|For example, showing a progress bar using the [`tqdm`](https://github.com/tqdm/tqdm) library.
239|
240|```python
241|import io
242|import random
243|
244|import httpx
245|from tqdm import tqdm
246|
247|
248|def gen():
249|    """
250|    this is a complete example with generated random bytes.
251|    you can replace `io.BytesIO` with real file object.
252|    """
253|    total = 32 * 1024 * 1024  # 32m
254|    with tqdm(ascii=True, unit_scale=True, unit='B', unit_divisor=1024, total=total) as bar:
255|        with io.BytesIO(random.randbytes(total)) as f:
256|            while data := f.read(1024):
257|                yield data
258|                bar.update(len(data))
259|
260|
261|httpx.post("https://httpbin.org/post", content=gen())
262|```
263|
264|![tqdm progress bar](../img/tqdm-progress.gif)
265|
266|## Multipart file encoding
267|
268|As mentioned in the [quickstart](../quickstart.md#sending-multipart-file-uploads)
269|multipart file encoding is available by passing a dictionary with the
270|name of the payloads as keys and either tuple of elements or a file-like object or a string as values.
271|
272|```pycon
273|>>> with open('report.xls', 'rb') as report_file:
274|...     files = {'upload-file': ('report.xls', report_file, 'application/vnd.ms-excel')}
275|...     r = httpx.post("https://httpbin.org/post", files=files)
276|>>> print(r.text)
277|{
278|  ...
279|  "files": {
280|    "upload-file": "<... binary content ...>"
281|  },
282|  ...
283|}
284|```
285|
286|More specifically, if a tuple is used as a value, it must have between 2 and 3 elements:
287|
288|- The first element is an optional file name which can be set to `None`.
289|- The second element may be a file-like object or a string which will be automatically
290|encoded in UTF-8.
291|- An optional third element can be used to specify the
292|[MIME type](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Basics_of_HTTP/MIME_Types)
293|of the file being uploaded. If not specified HTTPX will attempt to guess the MIME type based
294|on the file name, with unknown file extensions defaulting to "application/octet-stream".
295|If the file name is explicitly set to `None` then HTTPX will not include a content-type
296|MIME header field.
297|
298|```pycon
299|>>> files = {'upload-file': (None, 'text content', 'text/plain')}
300|>>> r = httpx.post("https://httpbin.org/post", files=files)
301|>>> print(r.text)
302|{
303|  ...
304|  "files": {},
305|  "form": {
306|    "upload-file": "text-content"
307|  },
308|  ...
309|}
310|```
311|
312|!!! tip
313|    It is safe to upload large files this way. File uploads are streaming by default, meaning that only one chunk will be loaded into memory at a time.
314|
315| Non-file data fields can be included in the multipart form using by passing them to `data=...`.
316|
317|You can also send multiple files in one go with a multiple file field form.
318|To do that, pass a list of `(field, <file>)` items instead of a dictionary, allowing you to pass multiple items with the same `field`.
319|For instance this request sends 2 files, `foo.png` and `bar.png` in one request on the `images` form field:
320|
321|```pycon
322|>>> with open('foo.png', 'rb') as foo_file, open('bar.png', 'rb') as bar_file:
323|...     files = [
324|...         ('images', ('foo.png', foo_file, 'image/png')),
325|...         ('images', ('bar.png', bar_file, 'image/png')),
326|...     ]
327|...     r = httpx.post("https://httpbin.org/post", files=files)
328|```

4|import itertools
5|import sys
6|import typing
7|
8|from .._models import Request, Response
9|from .._types import SyncByteStream
10|from .base import BaseTransport
11|
12|if typing.TYPE_CHECKING:
13|    from _typeshed import OptExcInfo  # pragma: no cover
14|    from _typeshed.wsgi import WSGIApplication  # pragma: no cover
15|
16|_T = typing.TypeVar("_T")
17|
18|
19|__all__ = ["WSGITransport"]
20|
21|
22|def _skip_leading_empty_chunks(body: typing.Iterable[_T]) -> typing.Iterable[_T]:
23|    body = iter(body)
24|    for chunk in body:
25|        if chunk:
26|            return itertools.chain([chunk], body)
27|    return []

30|class WSGIByteStream(SyncByteStream):
31|    def __init__(self, result: typing.Iterable[bytes]) -> None:
32|        self._close = getattr(result, "close", None)
33|        self._result = _skip_leading_empty_chunks(result)
34|
35|    def __iter__(self) -> typing.Iterator[bytes]:
36|        for part in self._result:
37|            yield part
38|
39|    def close(self) -> None:
40|        if self._close is not None:
41|            self._close()
42|

44|class WSGITransport(BaseTransport):
45|    """
46|    A custom transport that handles sending requests directly to an WSGI app.
47|    The simplest way to use this functionality is to use the `app` argument.
48|
49|    ```
50|    client = httpx.Client(app=app)
51|    ```
52|
53|    Alternatively, you can setup the transport instance explicitly.
54|    This allows you to include any additional configuration arguments specific
55|    to the WSGITransport class:
56|
57|    ```
58|    transport = httpx.WSGITransport(
59|        app=app,
60|        script_name="/submount",
61|        remote_addr="1.2.3.4"
62|    )
63|    client = httpx.Client(transport=transport)
64|    ```
65|
66|    Arguments:
67|
68|    * `app` - The WSGI application.
69|    * `raise_app_exceptions` - Boolean indicating if exceptions in the application
70|       should be raised. Default to `True`. Can be set to `False` for use cases
71|       such as testing the content of a client 500 response.
72|    * `script_name` - The root path on which the WSGI application should be mounted.
73|    * `remote_addr` - A string indicating the client IP of incoming requests.
74|    ```
75|    """
76|
77|    def __init__(
78|        self,
79|        app: WSGIApplication,
80|        raise_app_exceptions: bool = True,
81|        script_name: str = "",
82|        remote_addr: str = "127.0.0.1",
83|        wsgi_errors: typing.TextIO | None = None,
84|    ) -> None:
85|        self.app = app
86|        self.raise_app_exceptions = raise_app_exceptions
87|        self.script_name = script_name
88|        self.remote_addr = remote_addr
89|        self.wsgi_errors = wsgi_errors
90|
91|    def handle_request(self, request: Request) -> Response:
92|        request.read()
93|        wsgi_input = io.BytesIO(request.content)
94|
95|        port = request.url.port or {"http": 80, "https": 443}[request.url.scheme]
96|        environ = {
97|            "wsgi.version": (1, 0),
98|            "wsgi.url_scheme": request.url.scheme,
99|            "wsgi.input": wsgi_input,
100|            "wsgi.errors": self.wsgi_errors or sys.stderr,
101|            "wsgi.multithread": True,
102|            "wsgi.multiprocess": False,
103|            "wsgi.run_once": False,
104|            "REQUEST_METHOD": request.method,
105|            "SCRIPT_NAME": self.script_name,
106|            "PATH_INFO": request.url.path,
107|            "QUERY_STRING": request.url.query.decode("ascii"),
108|            "SERVER_NAME": request.url.host,
109|            "SERVER_PORT": str(port),
110|            "SERVER_PROTOCOL": "HTTP/1.1",
111|            "REMOTE_ADDR": self.remote_addr,
112|        }
113|        for header_key, header_value in request.headers.raw:
114|            key = header_key.decode("ascii").upper().replace("-", "_")
115|            if key not in ("CONTENT_TYPE", "CONTENT_LENGTH"):
116|                key = "HTTP_" + key
117|            environ[key] = header_value.decode("ascii")
118|
119|        seen_status = None
120|        seen_response_headers = None
121|        seen_exc_info = None
122|
123|        def start_response(
124|            status: str,
125|            response_headers: list[tuple[str, str]],
126|            exc_info: OptExcInfo | None = None,
127|        ) -> typing.Callable[[bytes], typing.Any]:
128|            nonlocal seen_status, seen_response_headers, seen_exc_info
129|            seen_status = status
130|            seen_response_headers = response_headers
131|            seen_exc_info = exc_info
132|            return lambda _: None
133|
134|        result = self.app(environ, start_response)
135|
136|        stream = WSGIByteStream(result)
137|
138|        assert seen_status is not None
139|        assert seen_response_headers is not None
140|        if seen_exc_info and seen_exc_info[0] and self.raise_app_exceptions:
141|            raise seen_exc_info[1]
142|
143|        status_code = int(seen_status.split()[0])
144|        headers = [
145|            (key.encode("ascii"), value.encode("ascii"))
146|            for key, value in seen_response_headers
147|        ]
148|
149|        return Response(status_code, headers=headers, stream=stream)

1|# Requests Compatibility Guide
2|
3|HTTPX aims to be broadly compatible with the `requests` API, although there are a
4|few design differences in places.
5|
6|This documentation outlines places where the API differs...
7|
8|## Redirects
9|
10|Unlike `requests`, HTTPX does **not follow redirects by default**.
11|
12|We differ in behaviour here [because auto-redirects can easily mask unnecessary network
13|calls being made](https://github.com/encode/httpx/discussions/1785).
14|
15|You can still enable behaviour to automatically follow redirects, but you need to
16|do so explicitly...
17|
18|```python
19|response = client.get(url, follow_redirects=True)
20|```
21|
22|Or else instantiate a client, with redirect following enabled by default...
23|
24|```python
25|client = httpx.Client(follow_redirects=True)
26|```
27|
28|## Client instances
29|
30|The HTTPX equivalent of `requests.Session` is `httpx.Client`.
31|
32|```python
33|session = requests.Session(**kwargs)
34|```
35|
36|is generally equivalent to
37|
38|```python
39|client = httpx.Client(**kwargs)
40|```
41|
42|## Request URLs
43|
44|Accessing `response.url` will return a `URL` instance, rather than a string.
45|
46|Use `str(response.url)` if you need a string instance.
47|
48|## Determining the next redirect request
49|
50|The `requests` library exposes an attribute `response.next`, which can be used to obtain the next redirect request.
51|
52|```python
53|session = requests.Session()
54|request = requests.Request("GET", ...).prepare()
55|while request is not None:
56|    response = session.send(request, allow_redirects=False)
57|    request = response.next
58|```
59|
60|In HTTPX, this attribute is instead named `response.next_request`. For example:
61|
62|```python
63|client = httpx.Client()
64|request = client.build_request("GET", ...)
65|while request is not None:
66|    response = client.send(request)
67|    request = response.next_request
68|```
69|
70|## Request Content
71|
72|For uploading raw text or binary content we prefer to use a `content` parameter,
73|in order to better separate this usage from the case of uploading form data.
74|
75|For example, using `content=...` to upload raw content:
76|
77|```python
78|# Uploading text, bytes, or a bytes iterator.
79|httpx.post(..., content=b"Hello, world")
80|```
81|
82|And using `data=...` to send form data:
83|
84|```python
85|# Uploading form data.
86|httpx.post(..., data={"message": "Hello, world"})
87|```
88|
89|Using the `data=<text/byte content>` will raise a deprecation warning,
90|and is expected to be fully removed with the HTTPX 1.0 release.
91|
92|## Upload files
93|
94|HTTPX strictly enforces that upload files must be opened in binary mode, in order
95|to avoid character encoding issues that can result from attempting to upload files
96|opened in text mode.
97|
98|## Content encoding
99|
100|HTTPX uses `utf-8` for encoding `str` request bodies. For example, when using `content=<str>` the request body will be encoded to `utf-8` before being sent over the wire. This differs from Requests which uses `latin1`. If you need an explicit encoding, pass encoded bytes explicitly, e.g. `content=<str>.encode("latin1")`.
101|For response bodies, assuming the server didn't send an explicit encoding then HTTPX will do its best to figure out an appropriate encoding. HTTPX makes a guess at the encoding to use for decoding the response using `charset_normalizer`. Fallback to that or any content with less than 32 octets will be decoded using `utf-8` with the `error="replace"` decoder strategy.
102|
103|## Cookies
104|
105|If using a client instance, then cookies should always be set on the client rather than on a per-request basis.
106|
107|This usage is supported:
108|
109|```python
110|client = httpx.Client(cookies=...)
111|client.post(...)
112|```
113|
114|This usage is **not** supported:
115|
116|```python
117|client = httpx.Client()
118|client.post(..., cookies=...)
119|```
120|
121|We prefer enforcing a stricter API here because it provides clearer expectations around cookie persistence, particularly when redirects occur.
122|
123|## Status Codes
124|
125|In our documentation we prefer the uppercased versions, such as `codes.NOT_FOUND`, but also provide lower-cased versions for API compatibility with `requests`.
126|
127|Requests includes various synonyms for status codes that HTTPX does not support.
128|
129|## Streaming responses
130|
131|HTTPX provides a `.stream()` interface rather than using `stream=True`. This ensures that streaming responses are always properly closed outside of the stream block, and makes it visually clearer at which points streaming I/O APIs may be used with a response.
132|
133|For example:
134|
135|```python
136|with httpx.stream("GET", "https://www.example.com") as response:
137|    ...
138|```
139|
140|Within a `stream()` block request data is made available with:
141|
142|* `.iter_bytes()` - Instead of `response.iter_content()`
143|* `.iter_text()` - Instead of `response.iter_content(decode_unicode=True)`
144|* `.iter_lines()` - Corresponding to `response.iter_lines()`
145|* `.iter_raw()` - Use this instead of `response.raw`
146|* `.read()` - Read the entire response body, making `response.text` and `response.content` available.
147|
148|## Timeouts
149|
150|HTTPX defaults to including reasonable [timeouts](quickstart.md#timeouts) for all network operations, while Requests has no timeouts by default.
151|
152|To get the same behavior as Requests, set the `timeout` parameter to `None`:
153|
154|```python
155|httpx.get('https://www.example.com', timeout=None)
156|```
157|
158|## Proxy keys
159|
160|HTTPX uses the mounts argument for HTTP proxying and transport routing.
161|It can do much more than proxies and allows you to configure more than just the proxy route.
162|For more detailed documentation, see [Mounting Transports](advanced/transports.md#mounting-transports).
163|
164|When using `httpx.Client(mounts={...})` to map to a selection of different transports, we use full URL schemes, such as `mounts={"http://": ..., "https://": ...}`.
165|
166|This is different to the `requests` usage of `proxies={"http": ..., "https": ...}`.
167|
168|This change is for better consistency with more complex mappings, that might also include domain names, such as `mounts={"all://": ..., httpx.HTTPTransport(proxy="all://www.example.com": None})` which maps all requests onto a proxy, except for requests to "www.example.com" which have an explicit exclusion.
169|
170|Also note that `requests.Session.request(...)` allows a `proxies=...` parameter, whereas `httpx.Client.request(...)` does not allow `mounts=...`.
171|
172|## SSL configuration
173|
174|When using a `Client` instance, the ssl configurations should always be passed on client instantiation, rather than passed to the request method.
175|
176|If you need more than one different SSL configuration, you should use different client instances for each SSL configuration.
177|
178|## Request body on HTTP methods
179|
180|The HTTP `GET`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`, and `OPTIONS` methods are specified as not supporting a request body. To stay in line with this, the `.get`, `.delete`, `.head` and `.options` functions do not support `content`, `files`, `data`, or `json` arguments.
181|
182|If you really do need to send request data using these http methods you should use the generic `.request` function instead.
183|
184|```python
185|httpx.request(
186|  method="DELETE",
187|  url="https://www.example.com/",
188|  content=b'A request body on a DELETE request.'
189|)
190|```
191|
192|## Checking for success and failure responses
193|
194|We don't support `response.is_ok` since the naming is ambiguous there, and might incorrectly imply an equivalence to `response.status_code == codes.OK`. Instead we provide the `response.is_success` property, which can be used to check for a 2xx response.
195|
196|## Request instantiation
197|
198|There is no notion of [prepared requests](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user/advanced/#prepared-requests) in HTTPX. If you need to customize request instantiation, see [Request instances](advanced/clients.md#request-instances).
199|
200|Besides, `httpx.Request()` does not support the `auth`, `timeout`, `follow_redirects`, `mounts`, `verify` and `cert` parameters. However these are available in `httpx.request`, `httpx.get`, `httpx.post` etc., as well as on [`Client` instances](advanced/clients.md#client-instances).
201|
202|## Mocking
203|
204|If you need to mock HTTPX the same way that test utilities like `responses` and `requests-mock` does for `requests`, see [RESPX](https://github.com/lundberg/respx).
205|
206|## Caching
207|
208|If you use `cachecontrol` or `requests-cache` to add HTTP Caching support to the `requests` library, you can use [Hishel](https://hishel.com) for HTTPX.
209|
210|## Networking layer
211|
212|`requests` defers most of its HTTP networking code to the excellent [`urllib3` library](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/latest/).
213|
214|On the other hand, HTTPX uses [HTTPCore](https://github.com/encode/httpcore) as its core HTTP networking layer, which is a different project than `urllib3`.
215|
216|## Query Parameters
217|
218|`requests` omits `params` whose values are `None` (e.g. `requests.get(..., params={"foo": None})`). This is not supported by HTTPX.
219|
220|For both query params (`params=`) and form data (`data=`), `requests` supports sending a list of tuples (e.g. `requests.get(..., params=[('key1', 'value1'), ('key1', 'value2')])`). This is not supported by HTTPX. Instead, use a dictionary with lists as values. E.g.: `httpx.get(..., params={'key1': ['value1', 'value2']})` or with form data: `httpx.post(..., data={'key1': ['value1', 'value2']})`.
221|
222|## Event Hooks
223|
224|`requests` allows event hooks to mutate `Request` and `Response` objects. See [examples](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/master/user/advanced/#event-hooks) given in the documentation for `requests`.
225|
226|In HTTPX, event hooks may access properties of requests and responses, but event hook callbacks cannot mutate the original request/response.
227|
228|If you are looking for more control, consider checking out [Custom Transports](advanced/transports.md#custom-transports).
229|
230|## Exceptions and Errors
231|
232|`requests` exception hierarchy is slightly different to the `httpx` exception hierarchy. `requests` exposes a top level `RequestException`, where as `httpx` exposes a top level `HTTPError`. see the exceptions exposes in requests [here](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/_modules/requests/exceptions/). See the `httpx` error hierarchy [here](https://www.python-httpx.org/exceptions/).

1|# Extensions
2|
3|Request and response extensions provide a untyped space where additional information may be added.
4|
5|Extensions should be used for features that may not be available on all transports, and that do not fit neatly into [the simplified request/response model](https://www.encode.io/httpcore/extensions/) that the underlying `httpcore` package uses as its API.
6|
7|Several extensions are supported on the request:
8|
9|```python
10|# Request timeouts actually implemented as an extension on
11|# the request, ensuring that they are passed throughout the
12|# entire call stack.
13|client = httpx.Client()
14|response = client.get(
15|    "https://www.example.com",
16|    extensions={"timeout": {"connect": 5.0}}
17|)
18|response.request.extensions["timeout"]
19|{"connect": 5.0}
20|```
21|
22|And on the response:
23|
24|```python
25|client = httpx.Client()
26|response = client.get("https://www.example.com")
27|print(response.extensions["http_version"])  # b"HTTP/1.1"
28|# Other server responses could have been
29|# b"HTTP/0.9", b"HTTP/1.0", or b"HTTP/1.1"
30|```
31|
32|## Request Extensions
33|
34|### `"trace"`
35|
36|The trace extension allows a callback handler to be installed to monitor the internal
37|flow of events within the underlying `httpcore` transport.
38|
39|The simplest way to explain this is with an example:
40|
41|```python
42|import httpx
43|
44|def log(event_name, info):
45|    print(event_name, info)
46|
47|client = httpx.Client()
48|response = client.get("https://www.example.com/", extensions={"trace": log})
49|# connection.connect_tcp.started {'host': 'www.example.com', 'port': 443, 'local_address': None, 'timeout': None}
50|# connection.connect_tcp.complete {'return_value': <httpcore.backends.sync.SyncStream object at 0x1093f94d0>}
51|# connection.start_tls.started {'ssl_context': <ssl.SSLContext object at 0x1093ee750>, 'server_hostname': b'www.example.com', 'timeout': None}
52|# connection.start_tls.complete {'return_value': <httpcore.backends.sync.SyncStream object at 0x1093f9450>}
53|# http11.send_request_headers.started {'request': <Request [b'GET']>}
54|# http11.send_request_headers.complete {'return_value': None}
55|# http11.send_request_body.started {'request': <Request [b'GET']>}
56|# http11.send_request_body.complete {'return_value': None}
57|# http11.receive_response_headers.started {'request': <Request [b'GET']>}
58|# http11.receive_response_headers.complete {'return_value': (b'HTTP/1.1', 200, b'OK', [(b'Age', b'553715'), (b'Cache-Control', b'max-age=604800'), (b'Content-Type', b'text/html; charset=UTF-8'), (b'Date', b'Thu, 21 Oct 2021 17:08:42 GMT'), (b'Etag', b'"3147526947+ident"'), (b'Expires', b'Thu, 28 Oct 2021 17:08:42 GMT'), (b'Last-Modified', b'Thu, 17 Oct 2019 07:18:26 GMT'), (b'Server', b'ECS (nyb/1DCD)'), (b'Vary', b'Accept-Encoding'), (b'X-Cache', b'HIT'), (b'Content-Length', b'1256')])}
59|# http11.receive_response_body.started {'request': <Request [b'GET']>}
60|# http11.receive_response_body.complete {'return_value': None}
61|# http11.response_closed.started {}
62|# http11.response_closed.complete {'return_value': None}
63|```
64|
65|The `event_name` and `info` arguments here will be one of the following:
66|
67|* `{event_type}.{event_name}.started`, `<dictionary of keyword arguments>`
68|* `{event_type}.{event_name}.complete`, `{"return_value": <...>}`
69|* `{event_type}.{event_name}.failed`, `{"exception": <...>}`
70|
71|Note that when using async code the handler function passed to `"trace"` must be an `async def ...` function.
72|
73|The following event types are currently exposed...
74|
75|**Establishing the connection**
76|
77|* `"connection.connect_tcp"`
78|* `"connection.connect_unix_socket"`
79|* `"connection.start_tls"`
80|
81|**HTTP/1.1 events**
82|
83|* `"http11.send_request_headers"`
84|* `"http11.send_request_body"`
85|* `"http11.receive_response"`
86|* `"http11.receive_response_body"`
87|* `"http11.response_closed"`
88|
89|**HTTP/2 events**
90|
91|* `"http2.send_connection_init"`
92|* `"http2.send_request_headers"`
93|* `"http2.send_request_body"`
94|* `"http2.receive_response_headers"`
95|* `"http2.receive_response_body"`
96|* `"http2.response_closed"`
97|
98|The exact set of trace events may be subject to change across different versions of `httpcore`. If you need to rely on a particular set of events it is recommended that you pin installation of the package to a fixed version.
99|
100|### `"sni_hostname"`
101|
102|The server's hostname, which is used to confirm the hostname supplied by the SSL certificate.
103|
104|If you want to connect to an explicit IP address rather than using the standard DNS hostname lookup, then you'll need to use this request extension.
105|
106|For example:
107|
108|``` python
109|# Connect to '185.199.108.153' but use 'www.encode.io' in the Host header,
110|# and use 'www.encode.io' when SSL verifying the server hostname.
111|client = httpx.Client()
112|headers = {"Host": "www.encode.io"}
113|extensions = {"sni_hostname": "www.encode.io"}
114|response = client.get(
115|    "https://185.199.108.153/path",
116|    headers=headers,
117|    extensions=extensions
118|)
119|```
120|
121|### `"timeout"`
122|
123|A dictionary of `str: Optional[float]` timeout values.
124|
125|May include values for `'connect'`, `'read'`, `'write'`, or `'pool'`.
126|
127|For example:
128|
129|```python
130|# Timeout if a connection takes more than 5 seconds to established, or if
131|# we are blocked waiting on the connection pool for more than 10 seconds.
132|client = httpx.Client()
133|response = client.get(
134|    "https://www.example.com",
135|    extensions={"timeout": {"connect": 5.0, "pool": 10.0}}
136|)
137|```
138|
139|This extension is how the `httpx` timeouts are implemented, ensuring that the timeout values are associated with the request instance and passed throughout the stack. You shouldn't typically be working with this extension directly, but use the higher level `timeout` API instead.
140|
141|### `"target"`
142|
143|The target that is used as [the HTTP target instead of the URL path](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2616#section-5.1.2).
144|
145|This enables support constructing requests that would otherwise be unsupported.
146|
147|* URL paths with non-standard escaping applied.
148|* Forward proxy requests using an absolute URI.
149|* Tunneling proxy requests using `CONNECT` with hostname as the target.
150|* Server-wide `OPTIONS *` requests.
151|
152|Some examples:
153|
154|Using the 'target' extension to send requests without the standard path escaping rules...
155|
156|```python
157|# Typically a request to "https://www.example.com/test^path" would
158|# connect to "www.example.com" and send an HTTP/1.1 request like...
159|#
160|# GET /test%5Epath HTTP/1.1
161|#
162|# Using the target extension we can include the literal '^'...
163|#
164|# GET /test^path HTTP/1.1
165|#
166|# Note that requests must still be valid HTTP requests.
167|# For example including whitespace in the target will raise a `LocalProtocolError`.
168|extensions = {"target": b"/test^path"}
169|response = httpx.get("https://www.example.com", extensions=extensions)
170|```
171|
172|The `target` extension also allows server-wide `OPTIONS *` requests to be constructed...
173|
174|```python
175|# This will send the following request...
176|#
177|# CONNECT * HTTP/1.1
178|extensions = {"target": b"*"}
179|response = httpx.request("CONNECT", "https://www.example.com", extensions=extensions)
180|```
181|
182|## Response Extensions
183|
184|### `"http_version"`
185|
186|The HTTP version, as bytes. Eg. `b"HTTP/1.1"`.
187|
188|When using HTTP/1.1 the response line includes an explicit version, and the value of this key could feasibly be one of `b"HTTP/0.9"`, `b"HTTP/1.0"`, or `b"HTTP/1.1"`.
189|
190|When using HTTP/2 there is no further response versioning included in the protocol, and the value of this key will always be `b"HTTP/2"`.
191|
192|### `"reason_phrase"`
193|
194|The reason-phrase of the HTTP response, as bytes. For example `b"OK"`. Some servers may include a custom reason phrase, although this is not recommended.
195|
196|HTTP/2 onwards does not include a reason phrase on the wire.
197|
198|When no key is included, a default based on the status code may be used.
199|
200|### `"stream_id"`
201|
202|When HTTP/2 is being used the `"stream_id"` response extension can be accessed to determine the ID of the data stream that the response was sent on.
203|
204|### `"network_stream"`
205|
206|The `"network_stream"` extension allows developers to handle HTTP `CONNECT` and `Upgrade` requests, by providing an API that steps outside the standard request/response model, and can directly read or write to the network.
207|
208|The interface provided by the network stream:
209|
210|* `read(max_bytes, timeout = None) -> bytes`
211|* `write(buffer, timeout = None)`
212|* `close()`
213|* `start_tls(ssl_context, server_hostname = None, timeout = None) -> NetworkStream`
214|* `get_extra_info(info) -> Any`
215|
216|This API can be used as the foundation for working with HTTP proxies, WebSocket upgrades, and other advanced use-cases.
217|
218|See the [network backends documentation](https://www.encode.io/httpcore/network-backends/) for more information on working directly with network streams.
219|
220|**Extra network information**
221|
222|The network stream abstraction also allows access to various low-level information that may be exposed by the underlying socket:
223|
224|```python
225|response = httpx.get("https://www.example.com")
226|network_stream = response.extensions["network_stream"]
227|
228|client_addr = network_stream.get_extra_info("client_addr")
229|server_addr = network_stream.get_extra_info("server_addr")
230|print("Client address", client_addr)
231|print("Server address", server_addr)
232|```
233|
234|The socket SSL information is also available through this interface, although you need to ensure that the underlying connection is still open, in order to access it...
235|
236|```python
237|with httpx.stream("GET", "https://www.example.com") as response:
238|    network_stream = response.extensions["network_stream"]
239|
240|    ssl_object = network_stream.get_extra_info("ssl_object")
241|    print("TLS version", ssl_object.version())
242|```
